passages.original: Ergo ille civis, qui id cogit omnis imperio legumque poena, quod vix paucis persuadere oratione philosophi possunt, etiam iis, qui illa disputant, ipsis est praeferendus doctoribus. Quae est enim istorum oratio tam exquisita, quae sit anteponenda bene constitutae civitati publico iure et moribus? Equidem quem ad modum urbes magnas atque imperiosas, ut appellat Ennius, viculis et castellis praeferendas puto, sic eos, qui his urbibus consilio atque auctoritate praesunt, iis, qui omnis negotii publici expertes sint, longe duco sapientia ipsa esse anteponendos. Et quoniam maxime rapimur ad opes augendas generis humani studemusque nostris consiliis et laboribus tutiorem et opulentiorem vitam hominum reddere et ad hanc voluptatem ipsius naturae stimulis incitamur, teneamus eum cursum, qui semper fuit optimi cuiusque, neque ea signa audiamus, quae receptui canunt, ut eos etiam revocent, qui iam processerint.
passages.english: Therefore the citizen who compels all men, by command and by the penalty of the laws, to do what philosophers can with difficulty persuade a few to do by speech, is to be preferred even to the very teachers who argue those things. For what discourse of theirs is so refined that it should be ranked above a state well established by public law and custom? For my part, just as I think that great and commanding cities, as Ennius calls them, are to be preferred to little villages and forts, so I consider that those who preside over these cities by counsel and authority are to be ranked far above those who have no part in any public business, even in wisdom itself. And since we are most strongly drawn to increase the resources of the human race, and are eager by our counsels and labours to make the life of men safer and richer, and are urged toward this pleasure by the goads of nature herself, let us hold to that course which has always been the course of all the best men, and let us not listen to those signals that sound the retreat, so as to call back even those who have already advanced.

passages.original: Dein Tubero: Nescio, Africane, cur ita memoriae proditum sit, Socratem omnem istam disputationem reiecisse et tantum de vita et de moribus solitum esse quaerere. Quem enim auctorem de illo locupletiorem Platone laudare possumus? cuius in libris multis locis ita loquitur Socrates, ut etiam, cum de moribus, de virtutibus, denique de re publica disputet, numeros tamen et geometriam et harmoniam studeat Pythagorae more coniungere. Tum Scipio: Sunt ista, ut dicis; sed audisse te credo, Tubero, Platonem Socrate mortuo primum in Aegyptum discendi causa, post in Italiam et in Siciliam contendisse, ut Pythagorae inventa perdisceret, eumque et cum Archyta Tarentino et cum Timaeo Locro multum fuisse et Philoleo commentarios esse nanctum, cumque eo tempore in iis locis Pythagorae nomen vigeret, illum se et hominibus Pythagoreis et studiis illis dedisse.
passages.english: Then Tubero [said]: I do not know, Africanus, why it has been handed down that Socrates rejected all that kind of inquiry and was accustomed to investigate only life and morals. For what richer authority on him can we cite than Plato? In whose books Socrates speaks in many places in such a way that, even when he is discussing morals, the virtues, and indeed the state, he is still eager to join to them numbers, geometry and harmony, in the manner of Pythagoras. Then Scipio [said]: It is as you say; but I believe you have heard, Tubero, that after the death of Socrates Plato went first to Egypt for the sake of learning, and afterwards to Italy and Sicily, in order to learn thoroughly the discoveries of Pythagoras; and that he spent much time with Archytas of Tarentum and with Timaeus of Locri, and obtained the notebooks of Philolaus; and that, since at that time the name of Pythagoras flourished in those places, he devoted himself both to the Pythagorean men and to those studies.

passages.original: Sed posteaquam coepit rationem huius operis scientissime Gallus exponere, plus in illo Siculo ingenii, quam videretur natura humana ferre potuisse, iudicavi fuisse. Dicebat enim Gallus sphaerae illius alterius solidae atque plenae vetus esse inventum, et eam a Thalete Milesio primum esse tornatam, post autem ab Eudoxo Cnidio, discipulo, ut ferebat, Platonis, eandem illam astris stellisque, quae caelo inhaererent, esse descriptam; cuius omnem ornatum et descriptionem sumptam ab Eudoxo multis annis post non astrologiae scientia, sed poetica quadam facultate versibus Aratum extulisse.
passages.english: But after Gallus began to explain the principle of this work with great expertise, I judged that there had been more genius in that Sicilian than human nature seemed able to bear. For Gallus said that the invention of that other, solid and full sphere was old, and that it had first been turned on a lathe by Thales of Miletus, but afterwards that same sphere had been marked out with the constellations and stars fixed in the sky by Eudoxus of Cnidus, a pupil, as he reported, of Plato; and that many years later Aratus, taking all its arrangement and description from Eudoxus, had set it forth in verse, not by knowledge of astronomy but by a certain poetic talent.
passages.notes: "That Sicilian" is Archimedes, named in the following context.

passages.original: Id autem postea ne nostrum quidem Ennium fugit; qui ut scribit, anno trecentesimo quinquagesimo fere post Romam conditam Nonis Iunis soli luna obstitit et nox. Atque hac in re tanta inest ratio atque sollertia, ut ex hoc die, quem apud Ennium et in maximis annalibus consignatum videmus, superiores solis defectiones reputatae sint usque ad illam, quae Nonis Quinctilibus fuit regnante Romulo; quibus quidem Romulum tenebris etiamsi natura ad humanum exitum abripuit, virtus tamen in caelum dicitur sustulisse.
passages.english: This, moreover, did not escape even our Ennius later; who writes that, about the three hundred and fiftieth year after the founding of Rome, on the Nones of June, the moon and night blocked the sun. And in this matter there is so much method and skill that, starting from this day, which we see recorded in Ennius and in the Great Annals, the earlier eclipses of the sun have been calculated back as far as the one that occurred on the Nones of Quinctilis in the reign of Romulus; and even if, in that darkness, nature carried Romulus off to a human end, yet his virtue is said to have raised him to heaven.
passages.notes: The 'anno trecentesimo quinquagesimo' figure is as transmitted; some editors emend it.

passages.original: qui inperia consulatusque nostros in necessariis, non in expetendis rebus, muneris fungendi gratia subeundos, non praemiorum aut gloriae causa adpetendos putet; qui denique, ut Africanum avum meum scribit Cato solitum esse dicere, possit idem de se praedicare, numquam se plus agere, quam nihil cum ageret, numquam minus solum esse, quam cum solus esset.
passages.english: who thinks that our commands and consulships are to be undertaken among necessary things, not among things to be sought, for the sake of performing a duty, not to be pursued for the sake of rewards or glory; who, finally, as Cato writes that my grandfather Africanus used to say, can declare the same of himself: that he was never doing more than when he was doing nothing, and never less alone than when he was alone.

passages.original: ut mihi Platonis illud, seu quis dixit alius, perelegans esse videatur; quem cum ex alto ignotas ad terras tempestas et in desertum litus detulisset, timentibus ceteris propter ignorationem locorum animadvertisse dicunt in arena geometricas formas quasdam esse descriptas;
passages.english: so that that saying of Plato's, or of whoever else said it, seems to me very elegant: when a storm had carried him from the open sea to unknown lands and onto a deserted shore, while the others were afraid because they did not know the place, he, they say, noticed certain geometrical figures drawn in the sand;

passages.original: in ipsius paterno genere fuit noster ille amicus, dignus huic ad imitandum, Egregie cordatus homo, catus Aelius Sextus, qui egregie cordatus et catus fuit et ab Ennio dictus est, non quod ea quaerebat, quae numquam inveniret, sed quod ea respondebat, quae eos, qui quaesissent, et cura et negotio solverent, cuique contra Galli studia disputanti in ore semper erat ille de Iphigenia Achilles: Ástrologorum sígna in caelo quíd fit observátionis,Cúm capra aut nepa aút exoritur nómen aliquod béluarum!Quód est ante pedes némo spectat, caéli scrutanúr plagas. Atque idem (multum enim illum audiebam et libenter) Zethum illum Pacuvii nimis inimicum doctrinae esse dicebat; magis eum delectabat Neoptolemus Ennii, qui se ait philosophari velle, sed paucis; nam omnino haud placere. Quodsi studia Graecorum vos tanto opere delectant, sunt alia liberiora et transfusa latius, quae vel ad usum vitae vel etiam ad ipsam rem publicam conferre possumus.
passages.english: …in his own father's family was that friend of ours, worthy for him to imitate, 'an outstandingly wise-hearted man, shrewd Aelius Sextus', who was outstandingly wise-hearted and shrewd, and was so called by Ennius, not because he sought things he would never find, but because he gave answers that freed those who had consulted him from both care and trouble; and when he argued against the studies of Gallus, he always had on his lips those words of Achilles in the Iphigenia: 'What is this observation of the astrologers' signs in the sky, when the Goat or the Scorpion or the name of some beast rises? No one looks at what is before his feet; we search the regions of the sky.' And the same man (for I used to listen to him often and gladly) used to say that Pacuvius' Zethus was too hostile to learning; he was better pleased by Ennius' Neoptolemus, who says he wishes to philosophise, but briefly, for to do so altogether does not please him. But if the studies of the Greeks delight you so greatly, there are others, more liberal and more widely spread, which we can apply either to the conduct of life or even to the state itself.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject of 'ipsius' and 'huic' is not given in the excerpt.

passages.original: facillimam autem in ea re publica esse concordiam, in qua idem conducat omnibus; ex utilitatis varietatibus, cum aliis aliud expediat, nasci discordias; itaque, cum patres rerum potirentur, numquam constitisse civitatis statum; multo iam id in regnis minus, quorum, ut ait Ennius, nulla regni sancta societas nec fides est. Quare cum lex sit civilis societatis vinculum, ius autem legis aequale, quo iure societas civium teneri potest, cum par non sit condicio civium? Si enim pecunias aequari non placet, si ingenia omnium paria esse non possunt, iura certe paria debent esse eorum inter se, qui sunt cives in eadem re publica.
passages.english: …[they say] that concord is easiest in that state in which the same thing benefits everyone; that from differences of interest, when one thing suits some and another thing others, discords arise; and that therefore, when the senators held power, the condition of the state never stood firm; and much less so in kingdoms, in which, as Ennius says, there is no sacred partnership or good faith of kingship. Therefore, since law is the bond of civil society, and the right established by law is equal, by what right can a society of citizens be held together when the condition of the citizens is not equal? For if it is not agreed that wealth should be equalised, and if the talents of all cannot be equal, then surely the rights of those who are citizens in the same state ought to be equal among themselves.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence in indirect speech reporting the democrats' view.

passages.original: Quid? inquit Laelius. Et ille: Quid censes, nisi quod est ante oculos? Sive haec ad utilitatem vitae constituta sunt a principibus rerum publicarum, ut rex putaretur unus esse in caelo, qui nutu, ut ait Homerus, totum Olympum converteret idemque et rex et pater haberetur omnium, magna auctoritas est multique testes, siquidem omnis multos appellari placet, ita consensisse gentes decretis videlicet principum, nihil esse rege melius, quoniam deos omnis censent unius regi numine;
passages.english: "What [do you mean]?" said Laelius. And he [replied]: "What do you think, except what is before our eyes? Whether these things were established by the leaders of states for the benefit of life, so that one king might be thought to be in heaven, who with a nod, as Homer says, turns all Olympus, and that he might be held to be both king and father of all, there is great authority and many witnesses, if indeed it is agreed to call 'all' 'many', that nations have so agreed, evidently by the decrees of their leaders, that nothing is better than a king, since they think all the gods are ruled by the divine will of one;
passages.notes: "si quidem omnis multos appellari placet" is obscure; the sense seems to be that the witnesses are all peoples, if 'all' may be counted as 'many'.

passages.original: iusto quidem rege cum est populus orbatus, pectora diu tenet desiderium, sicut ait Ennius, post optimi regis obitum; simul inter Sese sic memorant: o Romule, Romule die,Qualem te patriae custodem di genuerunt!O pater, o genitor, o sanguen dis oriundum! Non eros nec dominos appellabant eos, quibus iuste paruerunt, denique ne reges quidem, sed patriae custodes, sed patres, sed deos;
passages.english:
…indeed, when a people has been bereft of a just king, longing holds their hearts for a long time, as Ennius says, after the death of the best king; at the same time they say thus among themselves: 'O Romulus, divine Romulus,
what a guardian of the fatherland the gods begot in you!
O father, O begetter, O blood sprung from the gods!'
They did not call those whom they justly obeyed masters or lords, nor even kings, but guardians of the fatherland, fathers, gods;
passages.notes: 'die' read as 'dive' (divine), presumably a scanning error.

passages.original: Si quando aut regi iusto vim populus attulit regnove eum spoliavit aut etiam, id quod evenit saepius, optimatium sanguinem gustavit ac totam rem publicam substravit libidini suae (cave putes autem mare ullum aut flammam esse tantam, quam non facilius sit sedare quam effrenatam insolentia multitudinem), tum fit illud, quod apud Platonem est luculente dictum, si modo id exprimere Latine potuero; difficile factu est, sed conabor tamen.
passages.english: Whenever the people has either used violence against a just king or stripped him of his kingdom, or even, as happens more often, has tasted the blood of the aristocrats and laid the whole state beneath its own lust (and do not suppose that there is any sea or fire so great that it is not easier to calm than a multitude unbridled by insolence), then there occurs what is brilliantly said in Plato, if only I can express it in Latin; it is difficult to do, but I shall try nevertheless.

passages.original: libenter enim etiam verbo utor Catonis. Facilius autem, quod est propositum, consequar, si nostram rem publicam vobis et nascentem et crescentem et adultam et iam firmam atque robustam ostendero, quam si mihi aliquam, ut apud Platonem Socrates, ipse finxero.
passages.english: for I gladly use even Cato's word. And I shall more easily achieve what I have set out to do if I show you our own state at its birth, its growth, its maturity, and now firm and strong, than if I invent some state myself, as Socrates does in Plato.

passages.original: Nam si, id quod Graecorum investigatur annalibus, Roma condita est secundo anno Olympiadis septumae, in id saeculum Romuli cecidit aetas, cum iam plena Graecia poetarum et musicorum esset minorque fabulis nisi de veteribus rebus haberetur fides. Nam centum et octo annis postquam Lycurgus leges scribere instituit, prima posita est Olympias, quam quidam nominis errore ab eodem Lycurgo constitutam putant; Homerum autem, qui minimum dicunt, Lycurgi aetati triginta annis anteponunt fere.
passages.english: For if, as is ascertained from the annals of the Greeks, Rome was founded in the second year of the seventh Olympiad, the life of Romulus fell in that age when Greece was already full of poets and musicians, and less credence was given to fables except about ancient matters. For the first Olympiad was established one hundred and eight years after Lycurgus began to write his laws, which some, through a confusion of names, think was instituted by that same Lycurgus; and Homer, those who put him latest place about thirty years before the time of Lycurgus.

passages.original: reliqui disseruerunt sine ullo certo exemplari formaque rei publicae de generibus et de rationibus civitatum; tu mihi videris utrumque facturus; es enim ita ingressus, ut, quae ipse reperias, tribuere aliis malis quam, ut facit apud Platonem Socrates, ipse fingere et illa de urbis situ revoces ad rationem, quae a Romulo casu aut necessitate facta sunt, et disputes non vaganti oratione, sed defixa in una re publica. Quare perge, ut instituisti;
passages.english: the rest have discussed the kinds and principles of states without any definite model and form of a state; you seem to me about to do both; for you have begun in such a way that you prefer to attribute to others what you yourself discover, rather than invent it yourself as Socrates does in Plato, and to bring back to a rational principle those things about the city's site which were done by Romulus through chance or necessity, and to argue not in a wandering discourse but one fixed on a single state. So continue as you have begun;

passages.original: Nam quartum iam annum regnante Lucio Tarquinio Superbo Sybarim et Crotonem et in eas Italiae partis Pythagoras venisse reperitur; Olympias enim secunda et sexagesima eadem Superbi regni initium et Pythagorae declarat adventum.
passages.english: For it is found that Pythagoras came to Sybaris and Croton and those parts of Italy in the fourth year of the reign of Lucius Tarquinius Superbus; for the sixty-second Olympiad marks both the beginning of Superbus' reign and the arrival of Pythagoras.

passages.original: Quare prima sit haec forma et species et origo tyranni inventa nobis in ea re publica, quam auspicato Romulus condiderit, non in illa, quam, ut perscripsit Plato, sibi ipse Socrates tripertito illo in sermone depinxerit, ut, quem ad modum Tarquinius, non novam potestatem nactus, sed, quam habebat, usus iniuste totum genus hoc regiae civitatis everterit; sit huic oppositus alter, bonus et sapiens et peritus utilitatis dignitatisque civilis quasi tutor et procurator rei publicae;
passages.english: Therefore let this be the first form, appearance and origin of a tyrant discovered by us, in that state which Romulus founded after taking the auspices, not in the one which, as Plato recorded, Socrates himself depicted for himself in that famous three-part conversation, namely how Tarquinius, not by acquiring new power but by using unjustly the power he had, overthrew this whole kind of royal state; let there be set against him another, good and wise and skilled in the advantage and dignity of the citizens, as it were a guardian and steward of the state;
passages.notes: "tripertito illo in sermone" is uncertain in sense; possibly the three-part discussion in Plato's Republic.

passages.original: Deinde, ut cubitum discessimus, me et de via fessum, et qui ad multam noctem vigilassem, artior quam solebat somnus complexus est. Hic mihi (credo equidem ex hoc, quod eramus locuti; fit enim fere, ut cogitationes sermonesque nostri pariant aliquid in somno tale, quale de Homero scribit Ennius, de quo videlicet saepissime vigilans solebat cogitare et loqui) Africanus se ostendit ea forma, quae mihi ex imagine eius quam ex ipso erat notior; quem ubi agnovi, equidem cohorrui, sed ille: Ades, inquit, animo et omitte timorem, Scipio, et, quae dicam, trade memoriae.
passages.english: Then, when we had gone off to bed, a deeper sleep than usual embraced me, both tired from the journey and having stayed awake until late into the night. Here (I suppose indeed from what we had been talking about; for it commonly happens that our thoughts and conversations produce something in sleep of the kind Ennius writes about concerning Homer, about whom, evidently, he used very often to think and speak while awake) Africanus showed himself to me in that form which was better known to me from his portrait mask than from himself; when I recognised him, I shuddered, but he said: 'Be of good courage, and put aside fear, Scipio, and commit to memory what I shall say.'
